name: aprendeSQL
tagline: Spanish-language interactive SQL course where you run queries in the browser against practice datasets and get checked automatically.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The machinery here is genuinely cheap to rebuild: an in-browser SQL engine, a seeded schema, an editor, and a checker that compares your result set to the expected one. An agent can hand you that in an afternoon, and it will work offline with no accounts. What it cannot hand you is a curriculum that someone sequenced on purpose, in Spanish, with exercises that fail in instructive ways instead of random ones. You can ask a model to generate exercises and it will produce something usable but uneven, with the occasional wrong expected answer that you only discover while arguing with your own grader. So: build the sandbox, accept that the teaching part is now your job.
coreLoopDIY: A local browser app that loads a practice database, lets you write SQL against it, and grades your query by comparing its result set to a stored expected result.
requirements: Willingness to write or review your own exercise set
A seed dataset, either CSVs you like or one the agent generates
whatYouLose: A deliberately ordered curriculum instead of a pile of exercises
Explanations and hints written by someone who has watched beginners get stuck
Confidence that every expected answer is actually correct
Dialect coverage, real Postgres and SQL Server behave differently from a WASM engine
Any sense of progress or accountability beyond a localStorage counter
moatNotes: Course products are mostly editorial labor wearing a web app as a costume. The costume is free now; the labor is not.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the hard part of learning SQL is not having a query box, it is knowing which twenty things to practice and in what order, and being told clearly why your attempt was wrong. A paid course is someone else having already made those decisions, in your language, with the dead ends removed. If you build the sandbox yourself you will spend your learning time debugging your grader instead of learning joins, which is a fun afternoon and a bad trade.
notes: The query sandbox is a one-sitting build; the lesson order is the actual product.
prompt:
Build a local, offline SQL practice app. No accounts, no backend, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable: Vite + React + TypeScript, Tailwind for styling, CodeMirror 6 with the SQL language mode for the editor, and sql.js (SQLite compiled to WASM) running entirely in the browser. No server, no Docker, no API keys, no .env needed.

Data: on app load, create an in-memory SQLite database and seed it from a single file src/data/schema.sql that you write. Use a small fictional store: customers, products, orders, order_items, employees. Around 60 rows total, with deliberate nulls, a few duplicate names, and dates spanning two years so that GROUP BY, HAVING, LEFT JOIN and date filtering all have something to bite on. Print the schema in a collapsible sidebar panel with column names and types.

Exercises: src/data/exercises.ts exports an array of objects: id, title, prompt (in Spanish), starterSql, solutionSql, and an optional hint. Write 20 exercises ordered by difficulty: SELECT and WHERE, ORDER BY and LIMIT, aggregates, GROUP BY plus HAVING, inner joins, left joins and null handling, subqueries, CTEs, window functions.

Grading: do NOT compare query text. Run the user's SQL and the solution SQL, then compare result sets. Column order and row order must match only if the exercise prompt mentions ordering, otherwise sort both result sets canonically before comparing. Compare values loosely for numbers (small epsilon) and treat null consistently. On failure show a side by side diff of expected vs actual rows, capped at 20 rows, plus the first mismatching cell. Never reveal solutionSql unless the user clicks a clearly labeled "ver solución" button.

UI: left pane exercise list with pass/fail state, center pane prompt plus editor plus a Run button (Cmd+Enter), bottom pane results table or the SQLite error message verbatim. Progress persists in localStorage. Add a "modo libre" tab that is just the editor against the same database with no grading.

In scope: everything above, a README with npm install and npm run dev, and vitest tests that assert every solutionSql passes its own grader.
Out of scope: user accounts, hosted deployment, multiple SQL dialects, a backend, AI hints, spaced repetition.
All user facing strings in Spanish. Keep it under 1500 lines.
